candidates.title: China’s institution-building amidst (dynamic) network effects: how will the relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions evolve?
candidates.abstract: How will the regime complex of balance-of-payments lending evolve amidst ongoing global power shifts? In this paper, we challenge the hitherto static outlook on the viability of external institutional change within the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) institutional environment. Dominant views in International Political Economy suggest that the IMF’s current focality will persist as China’s reformist approach to balance-of-payments lending and strong network effects favoring the IMF induce (inter-)institutional inertia. In contrast, we argue that the interests of challenger states – particularly China – and their exposure to network effects are dynamic. Depending on challengers’ evolving reformist or revisionist interests and their dynamic exposure to network effects, we derive pathways for external institutional change toward multiple inter-institutional relations between the IMF and newcomer institutions. Based on theoretical extrapolation and empirical trends, we claim that institutional hedging is a probable pathway for China’s institution-building efforts in the near future. For the more distant future, we introduce complementary layering and conflictual counter-institutionalization as highly contingent possibilities and discuss how the (inter-)actions of challengers and defenders during the hedging phase may shape their (non-)materialization. We thereby offer a methodologically innovative and policy-relevant outlook on future institutional change in international finance.

candidates.title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
candidates.abstract: Abstract In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.

candidates.title: New Evidence on the Demographics of the Paraguayan War: Revisiting Competing Estimates with Archival Draft Records
candidates.abstract: Abstract The demographic consequences of the Paraguayan War (1864–1870) remain among the most contested in Latin American history, with estimates of population loss ranging from under 20 percent to nearly 70 percent. This article revisits the debate by introducing newly digitized wartime administrative records from the Sección Nueva Encuadernación of the Archivo Nacional de Asunción, documenting draft-eligible males across forty-five districts in late 1867 and early 1868. Linking these records to prewar census benchmarks through a transparent projection methodology, I find that across the forty-two districts with a usable projected denominator, only 10,628 draft-eligible males aged twelve and older were observed against a projected male population of 100,692—roughly one in nine. The result is robust to alternative growth assumptions. Although male absence may reflect death, service, imprisonment, desertion, or displacement, the severity of late-war male scarcity is difficult to reconcile with low-loss interpretations and aligns closely with high-loss scenarios.

candidates.title: Trade-Offs in Authoritarian Participatory Digital Surveillance: Evidence From China’s Sharp Eyes Project
candidates.abstract: How do authoritarian regimes overcome the limits of digital surveillance? They complement camera systems with citizen monitoring and reporting, creating participatory surveillance in which residents interpret what cameras capture and supply local knowledge technology alone cannot provide. I study this hybrid form of control in China’s Sharp Eyes Project, which gives selected residents access to camera feeds and encourages reports of suspected misconduct. I use a staggered difference-in-differences analysis of administrative and survey data from Chinese cities. The program increases citizen reporting by 11%, reduces crimes susceptible to community monitoring, and lowers trust in neighbors. Reports expand the state’s informational reach, but the system makes residents uncertain about how neighbors may interpret and report their behavior. The study places political participation at the center of digital surveillance and shows how authoritarian regimes turn relations among citizens into a source of state power while weakening the foundations of collective action.

candidates.title: Preferences for the Poorest: New Data and Sectoral Evidence on Non-Reciprocal Trade
candidates.abstract: Non-reciprocal preferential trade arrangements (PTAs), such as the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP), are the main trade policy instrument for developing countries. Yet, existing data track changes in eligibility only coarsely and evidence on their effects is mixed. We introduce a database of 38 schemes (1950–2025) coding graduations, suspensions, and lapses. Structural gravity analysis finds no significant average effect, and none for beneficiaries other than least developed countries (LDCs). For LDCs, preferences raise exports to grantors by 34 percent, and GSP preferences by 88 percent. These gains concentrate in apparel and footwear and are not captured by tariffs.

candidates.title: Protestantism and insurance—an elective affinity? A multilevel comparative-historical analysis of the confessional insurance gap
candidates.abstract: Abstract While there are many studies and theories about the rise of social insurance and the public welfare state, the prior emergence and growth of private life and nonlife insurance are largely understudied, mostly due to a lack of data. This article fills this gap by testing whether there is an elective affinity between the rise and evolution of private insurance and Protestantism that is irreducible to typical factors external to religion (gross domestic product, education, demography, public welfare). Drawing on multiple new datasets, the paper tests whether Catholic–Protestant differences in insurance demand persist when controlling for standard covariates external to religion across nineteen OECD countries (1870–2020), across states in the confessionally mixed federations of Germany, Switzerland and the USA (1876–2020) as well as across US counties and European cities around 1909. The article finds Lutheran and Reformed Protestant areas to have had higher private insurance penetration and density than Catholic ones, controlling for standard covariates. This relationship is more pronounced in life than nonlife branches, more pronounced for insurance demand than insurance company activity, and more consistently found in Europe than within the USA. More generally, the article suggests that the confessional insurance gap may provide a missing empirical link to better understand the emergence of Alpine and Maritime insurance cultures, different premodern poor-ethics traditions and the different worlds of modern welfare states and pension systems.

candidates.title: Optimal avoidability in cross-border minimum taxation
candidates.abstract: Many tax regimes collect revenue to the extent that other governments do not. This paper develops a theory of how such cross-border minimum taxes should be designed, focusing on choices that affect avoidance of the regime. Making a minimum tax more difficult to avoid retains more firms within the regime but weakens competition among tax havens. Havens then raise their rates toward the minimum, reducing the top-up tax rate on shifted profit. As a result, an avoidable minimum tax can raise more revenue for the governments that impose it than an unavoidable one.

candidates.title: The populist contagion: how the mainstreaming of right-wing populist rhetoric reduces public support for international aid
candidates.abstract: This article examines whether the diffusion of populist rhetoric from populist to mainstream parties reduces public support for international organisations (IOs) and multilateral aid. We argue that when mainstream parties adopt populist anti-IO rhetoric, support for aid decreases not just amongst citizens, which hold populist attitudes and support populist parties, but also among more moderate voters. To test this cueing argument, we ran a survey experiment in France, Germany, Poland, Spain, and Sweden (n = 10,513) in early 2026. Varying both the message and the messenger, the experiment reveals, first, that populist anti-IO cues, indeed, reduce support for multilateral aid. Second, the messenger matters – while populist cues from populist parties primarily affect ideologically like-minded citizens, populist rhetoric voiced by mainstream parties reduces support across the political spectrum. Third, anti-IO rhetoric specifically undermines multilateral forms of aid while leaving support for bilateral aid unchanged. In sum, our study demonstrates how the normalisation of populist rhetoric by mainstream parties jeopardises public support for multilateral responses to transboundary risks and crises. Moreover, our findings underline that the populist contestation of IOs and multilateral aid is conceptually distinct from deservingness perceptions of the global poor.

candidates.title: Expected shortfall estimation and capital coverage under overlapping scenarios
candidates.abstract: Expected shortfall (ES) is routinely estimated from a short sample of profit-and-loss (P&L) scenarios built from overlapping multi-day returns, while the non-parametric estimators applied to such data are designed under independent sampling. We study how this mismatch affects estimation accuracy and capital coverage, and how it interacts with serial dependence and heavy tails in the underlying P&L. Working within the coherent risk estimation framework, we compare six order-statistic-based ES estimators on fit, bias, and capital-coverage metrics. Following the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB), we use a one-year estimation window and ES at the $2.5\%$ confidence level as a benchmark setup. We combine simulations with market data on twelve risk factors and ninety-nine equity portfolios. We show that overlapping sampling does not merely add noise but shifts ES estimates systematically downward, thereby weakening capital coverage. Serial dependence acts in the same direction, and heavy tails amplify both effects. More conservative weighting mitigates the underestimation but does not remove it. On market data, the confidence level at which the estimated capital covers realized losses roughly doubles in median under overlapping sampling for every estimator, while the $\textrm{ES}_{2.5\%}$-to-$\textrm{VaR}_{1\%}$ ratio, which links the FRTB base market risk capital metric to its pre-FRTB predecessor, changes comparatively little. Overlapping sampling can thus substantially understate ES-based capital. Since many banks apply a small set of standard estimators in their FRTB regulatory or economic capital model in a historical simulation approach, this understatement is likely to be common for many institutions, and combining simulation-based assessment of estimation risk with coverage-based diagnostics offers a practical method to detect it in model validation and monitoring.

candidates.title: Europe Adrift
candidates.abstract: Europe is adrift in the face of great turmoil and transformation. The liberal international order that emerged after the Cold War has disintegrated and the EU lacks a coherent strategic vision for responding to – let alone shaping – the emergent world order. There has been a shift away from market liberalism and toward state interventionism, strategic autonomy and a more assertive EU internationally. Yet these efforts are haunted by legacies from the neoliberal era that continue to limit its capacity for effective action. Herein lies the challenge. Europe struggles to overcome internal challenges, namely internal rivalry and a seeming inability to implement much-needed reforms, while it simultaneously faces a security threat from Russia, erratic mercantilism from the US, a competitiveness challenge vis-à-vis China, and declining goodwill in the Global South, all in the context of ecological collapse. This special issue takes the dynamics of intensifying global inter-state competition as an entry point to survey the erosion of European security, growth and normative power whose foundations were laid in the neoliberal era, the contradictions contestations and constraints revealed in the responses from European actors in the face of this erosion, and how European power and prosperity is being reshaped in unexpected ways.

candidates.title: The Value of Ignorance: Behavioral Preferences for Genetic Information and Insurance Market Equilibria
candidates.abstract: We study how behavioral heterogeneity in preferences for information acquisition affects equilibrium outcomes in health insurance markets. Individuals differ in the psychological utility they derive from learning information about their health risks, generating heterogeneous demand for genetic testing even when tests are inexpensive. The value of becoming informed depends on the insurance contracts available, while these contracts themselves depend on the fraction of individuals who acquire information. Information acquisition and insurance-market outcomes are therefore jointly determined. We show that these behavioral differences shape both the extent of adverse selection and whether the equilibrium is pooling or separating. Within a given contractual regime, stronger attraction to chance reduces information acquisition and mitigates adverse selection; in turn, it expands the range of testing costs for which the Wilson-type criterion selects pooling. Moreover, cheaper access to genetic information need not be associated with greater equilibrium information acquisition. At the testing-cost threshold at which the equilibrium switches from pooling to separation, the separating equilibrium prevailing at lower testing costs can exhibit a lower testing rate than the pooling equilibrium prevailing at slightly higher costs. Thus, the effect of technological progress on information acquisition depends on its endogenous impact on insurance contracts and equilibrium selection.

candidates.title: Do Transfer Tax Cuts Create Homeowners?
candidates.abstract: We study whether financial assistance to prospective homebuyers succeeds in promoting homeownership by analyzing a prominent real-estate transfer tax exemption for young homebuyers in the Netherlands. The reform offers quasi-experimental variation across time, buyers, and units, which we exploit using granular administrative data and various complementary reduced-form approaches. The two-percentage-point transfer tax cut substantially raised transactions among the young, but we can rule out even modest medium-run increases in homeownership. Instead, we document large timing and bunching responses. Prices of qualifying units increased by between 1.2% and 1.8%, suggesting that the tax cut mostly benefitted sellers. Welfare simulations reveal that, while the tax cut reduced transfer tax distortions and increased overall economic surplus, gains accrued primarily to upper-middle-income households.

candidates.title: Andean Glaciers in Times of Planetary Crisis
candidates.abstract: Abstract This special dossier examines how understandings of Andean glaciers transform under the planetary crisis, defined by humanity’s impact on geophysical processes at a planetary scale. Once regarded as remnants of deep geological time, glaciers have become emblematic casualties of anthropogenic global warming, their accelerated melting compressing geological history into human timescales and raising urgent ethical and political questions about protection, mitigation, and loss. This interdisciplinary collection, including contributions focused on Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, and the wider region, calls for approaches that move beyond universalizing Anthropocene narratives and toward historically and territorially situated accounts of glacial change, challenging colonial and extractivist frameworks that have long shaped the governance of ice and nature. The introduction argues that dominant scientific and state-centered framings—rooted in objectivity, distant observation, and a physicochemical definition of ice—tend to abstract glaciers into universal, placeless indicators of global change, obscuring the local extractivist and colonial dynamics driving their destruction, particularly through mining of critical minerals for a green energy transition. Against this detached view, the dossier foregrounds situated, relational, and often Indigenous conceptions of glaciers as vital entities embedded in organic, social, and spiritual life.

candidates.title: Contested elections and the power of new voters: The impact of extending voting rights to non-citizens
candidates.abstract: This paper examines the redistributive consequences of extending voting rights to non-citizens. We hypothesize that the fiscal response to such reforms depends on their capacity to alter the political status quo, particularly in closely contested constituencies. Using municipal-level data, we study the 1975 Swedish electoral reform, which granted non-citizens the right to vote in local elections. Our analysis reveals a one-time spike in municipal income taxes following the reform, with larger rises in municipalities with higher foreign-voter ratios. This increase in taxes was concentrated in municipalities where the vote margin between the two traditional political blocs in the previous election was narrow. These results highlight the central role of electoral competition in shaping the fiscal consequences of suffrage extensions and contribute to our understanding of how immigration interacts with local governance.

candidates.title: The Main Monetary Policy Shock
candidates.abstract: We propose a novel procedure to identify a main monetary policy (MMP) shock as the linear combination of monetary policy surprises that best explains macroeconomic fluctuations. Implemented with two standard high-frequency yield-curve surprises and the Boehm and Kroner (2024) non-yield shock, the MMP shock explains nontrivial business-cycle variation over the last 30 years, in contrast with prior findings. Moreover, the MMP shock differs markedly from a textbook monetary policy shock: a contractionary shock leaves interest rates mostly unchanged but persistently lowers headline prices and appreciates the dollar, while temporarily tightening financial conditions and depressing industrial production.

candidates.title: State-Building at What Cost? The Consequences of Military Control in Medieval China
candidates.abstract: A key challenge to state-building in conflict-prone societies is the proliferation of autonomous armed groups. As governments seek to enhance their monopoly over violence, the consequences of military centralization deserve scholarly attention. We argue that centralization produces mixed impacts on state's coercive capacity: by weakening the leaders of armed groups, it improves (undermines) political order at the upper (grassroots) level, and erodes military efficiency and discipline. Empirically, we leverage a centralization reform in China's Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE) after a civil war, using unique data on soldier mutinies, rebellions by local generals, civilian uprisings, and battle outcomes. Difference-indifferences estimates reveal that centralization successfully reduced local generals' rebellions, but led to increased soldier-led mutinies against the generals and more civilian uprisings. It also worsened battlefield performance. While research on state capacity has focused on its extractive and administrative dimensions, these findings deepen our understanding about another important aspect: the coercive dimension.

candidates.title: How Do Top Earners Respond to Taxation? Own- and Cross-Tax Base Responses, Efficiency, and Inequality
candidates.abstract: This paper presents new evidence on how top income earners respond to changes in the personal labor income tax schedule, uncovering both own- and cross-tax base responses within a unified framework. For identification, we exploit a 2012 tax reform in Uruguay that generated quasi-random variation in top marginal rates within the top 1% of the labor income distribution. Our empirical approach relies on a difference-in-differences identification strategy and administrative records linked at the individual level across multiple tax bases. We estimate an own-tax base intensive margin elasticity of 0.82 and extensive margin semi-elasticity of 3.36. Extensive margin responses are mostly driven by taxpayers shifting from the personal labor income tax base toward corporate income or capital income tax bases (semi-elasticities of -1.00 and -0.61, respectively). Our preferred estimates suggest that the reform was effective in increasing tax revenues, with efficiency costs representing 31% of the projected increase. However, it had limited impact on inequality, most likely due to its narrow scope and income shifting toward tax bases with lower and flat rates. Overall, our results indicate that policy efforts aiming to reduce inequality by increasing top marginal tax rates should also focus on limiting income shifting opportunities to strengthen their redistributive effects.

candidates.title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
candidates.abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)
institutions: The University of Texas at Austin

candidates.title: Offshoring and voting patterns in the US
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the impact of offshoring by US firms on voting patterns in the US. Using county-level voting data combined with industry-level offshoring data, we ask whether an increase in employment at foreign affiliates of US multinationals in vertically oriented industries is associated with an increase in the vote share for the incumbent party candidate in Presidential, House, and Senate elections. We find that offshoring leads to an increase in the incumbent vote share for counties with more educated workers, and a decrease for counties with higher shares of workers in the manufacturing sector and in occupations that are more easily relocated abroad. These results are consistent with the labor market literature on offshoring, which shows that offshoring has heterogeneous effects on workers’ employment based on skill and occupational tasks. This suggests that voters respond to the economic effects of offshoring by rewarding or punishing incumbent party candidates.
institutions: Center for Economic and Policy Research

candidates.title: Judicial performance and public procurement choice
candidates.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates whether judicial performance influences the choice of procurement procedures adopted by public authorities. Using data on Italian municipal public works contracts between 2009 and 2012, it examines the choice between negotiated procedures and formal tendering mechanisms in a range where both options were legally available. Identification relies on a spatial discontinuity design that exploits exogenous variation in judicial delay across court jurisdictions, further refined through intra-regional border comparisons and coarsened exact matching. The results show that longer judicial delays significantly reduce the likelihood of using negotiated procedures and increase the use of formal auctions. Consistent with a growing body of literature showing that inefficient courts increase contractual uncertainty, we argue that poor judicial performance shifts procurement choices toward highly formalized procurement mechanisms rather than more discretionary and market-oriented forms of contracting. In this sense, formal procurement procedures may partially compensate for weak judicial enforcement by shifting transaction governance toward greater ex-ante specification, procedural control, and verifiability. More broadly, the paper suggests that judicial ineffectiveness may contribute to the expansion of bureaucratic controls, shifting governance away from market-based arrangements and toward increasingly proceduralized administrative structures.

candidates.title: How does Coethnicity with Refugees Shape their Reception? Evidence from Afghan Refugees in Pakistan
candidates.abstract: How does coethnicity shape host attitudes toward refugees? Existing research often assumes that refugees who share the ethnic or cultural background of host populations will face less backlash. We test this assumption in Pakistan, where both refugee and host communities include substantial Pashtun populations. Drawing on original survey experimental, observational, and qualitative data, we find that while coethnicity increases refugee acceptance on average, this result masks sharp internal variation. Coethnic hosts who live in provinces where they are ethnic minorities are far more likely to express inclusive attitudes than those living in their ethnic homeland. The impact of coethnicity therefore depends on local context: in settings where ethnic identity is politically salient and shaped by marginalization, coethnicity with refugees can carry both instrumental and symbolic value. These findings complicate standard assumptions about the primacy of cultural threat and underscore the need to attend to subnational variation in refugee-host dynamics.

candidates.title: National Narratives in Comparative Politics: Theories, Methods, and Insights From Asia
candidates.abstract: In this introduction to the special issue, we define and explore the concept of national narratives in East and Southeast Asia. First, we define national narratives as collectively shared stories about a nation’s origins, boundaries and purposes. Second, we discuss three undertheorized elements of the narrative: the identity of the storyteller, the content of the stories, and contestation over the dominant narrative. Finally, we assess some methodological and measurement challenges in the literature before introducing the papers in this special issue. Drawing on cases from China, Vietnam, Indonesia, South Korea, Taiwan, Myanmar and the Philippines, we address questions related to the construction of personality cults and colonial memory. We also discuss how democratization impacts the identity of the storytellers, and how this impacts views on national boundaries and political violence.

candidates.title: Counterfactual assessment of social media interventions by separating exposure from engagement
candidates.abstract: Social media interventions are usually evaluated in individual-level experiments, which are costly to scale and often miss collective effects. We propose the Exposure--Engagement model, whose parameters separately control what social media users are exposed to (recommendation) and how they engage (behaviour). After fitting it to the Italian Twitter debate (2018--2022), we validate it at individual and collective levels. We simulate behavioural interventions (prebunking and accuracy prompts), calibrated on effect sizes, and a recommender-system intervention (chronological feed), comparing effects on engagement, attention diversity, and segregation. All three reduce engagement. Behavioural interventions slightly reduce diversity, leaving segregation unchanged, whereas the chronological feed increases diversity and reduces segregation. For these interventions, changing recommendation does more for the debate's structure than changing behaviour. We design a recommender-system intervention that increases engagement and diversity while reducing segregation, although with about a tenth of the chronological feed's gains, showing the framework's potential for pro-social intervention design.

candidates.title: Bulwarks or Enablers? Political Elites’ Attitudes to Political Candidates with Armed Group Linkages
candidates.abstract: Many elections feature candidates with ties to violent groups, yet little is known about the nomination stage. To understand whether political elites serve as gatekeepers against such candidates or whether other desirable traits lead selectors to overlook violent linkages, we study selectors’ preferences in candidate selection. Using an experiment with 11,392 Colombian local political elites, we examine how alleged armed group collusion is weighed against experience, track-records, popular support, and endorsements. We find that candidates with rumored armed group ties face a significant penalty in selectors’ evaluations. Some attributes, particularly experience, reduce this penalty, but none fully offset it. Candidates with ties to armed groups are also less rewarded for strong performance, suggesting that violent linkages diminish returns to otherwise desirable qualities. These findings indicate that the prevalence of violence-linked candidates is not primarily driven by selectors’ willingness to accommodate them, redirecting attention toward concealed linkages and constrained candidate pools.

candidates.title: HEARSAYBENCH: Can AI Navigate from Abstract Human Rights to Lived Lives?
candidates.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) reach users worldwide, personal counseling has emerged as one of their most consequential applications, sometimes in life-critical situations. Yet broader access does not mean equal support. The text these models learn from disproportionately reflects people with the freedom to act, embedding an implicit assumption that users can leave, report, seek help, or appeal. Existing benchmarks largely inherit this assumption, overlooking users whose agency is constrained by structural conditions such as war, statelessness, and displacement. Meanwhile, models are increasingly shaped by normative frameworks such as Constitutional AI, often grounded in ideals like human rights, even as many users live where those rights offer little protection or recourse. We introduce HEARSAYBENCH, a human-authored dataset of 400 test cases with in-region human verification grounded in scenarios where structural barriers stand between a person and the exercise of their rights. Built from United Nations and other human rights reports, the scenarios span over 80 regions and cover social, environmental, and personal constraints. Drawing on Nobel laureate Amartya Sen's Capabilities Approach, HEARSAYBENCH tests whether models can distinguish what a person is formally entitled to do from what they are actually able to do. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, every model infers a user's situation more accurately than it advises on it. Stronger models narrow this gap, but their recommendations remain unsafe to follow. Models may understand lives shaped by constraint, yet that knowledge remains hearsay if it cannot translate into advice people can act on. Those people are not alignment's long tail; they are among the users for whom good guidance matters most. HEARSAYBENCH makes this failure measurable, a step toward systems that serve the world as it is rather than as assumed.

candidates.title: Geopolitics and the EU-Australia Trade Agreement
candidates.abstract: Geopolitics is often seen as a risk for trade. This article shows how geopolitics can also increase trade openness: issue linkage with security can enable previously elusive trade compromises. In March 2026, the EU and Australia concluded negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA). The EU’s insistence for Australia to protect EU Geographical Indication (GI) food names such as Feta and Prosecco contributed to a repeated Australian walkout in 2023, suggesting an FTA was not feasible. However, in 2026 an FTA was concluded after all, alongside a Security and Defense Partnership. This article hypothesizes that US President Trump’s lack of reliability brought the EU and Australia closer together, pushing them to find detailed compromises to enable the conclusion of an FTA. Empirically, it leverages a survey experiment with 800 Australian voters and an analysis of GI provisions. The empirics are consistent with geopolitics having facilitated the trade deal, and “America First” politics contributing to middle power alliance-seeking such as between the EU and Australia, or the EU and Canada.

candidates.title: The cultural roots of state-owned enterprises: evidence from Europe
candidates.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the cultural roots of state ownership of enterprises. Drawing on data for European countries, we show that the scale of state ownership of enterprises is smaller in individualist societies than in collectivist ones. This relationship is robust to a broad set of cultural, economic, and historical controls. We address endogeneity concerns by using genetic, epidemiological, and linguistic data as instruments for individualism. We propose several political economy mechanisms underlying this relationship. First, in collectivist societies, voter preferences are tilted toward more extensive state ownership of enterprises. Second, in collectivist societies, interest groups may be stronger and democracy may be weaker, both of which can result in a larger share of state-owned enterprises in the economy. We provide empirical evidence supporting these channels. Finally, we show that the negative relationship between individualism and the scale of state ownership also holds in non-European countries.
institutions: Poznań University of Economics and Business

candidates.title: GESIS Surf: An Open-Source Infrastructure for Privacy-Preserving Longitudinal Web Browsing Data Collection
candidates.abstract: Understanding how people navigate digital media environments requires behavioral data beyond survey self-reports. However, existing infrastructures for collecting such data reproducibly, sustainably, and with strong privacy guarantees remain limited: commercial solutions lack transparency and data governance, while academic tools are typically designed for narrow, short-term use cases and do not support general-purpose academic panel data collections. We address this gap with GESIS Surf, a research infrastructure for large-scale longitudinal collection of web behavioral data in naturalistic environments. The system consists of a browser extension (Chrome and Firefox), a backend with a REST application programming interface (API), and a relational database. It passively captures user interactions, page metadata, and full HTML snapshots of each rendered page, embedding each observation within a hierarchical session model that preserves the structure of browsing behavior. GESIS Surf implements privacy-by-design through strict opt-in participation, per-domain collection rules, and client-side data minimization, ensuring that sensitive data are controlled at the point of collection. The system has been deployed with more than 1,000 participants in a large-scale academic panel infrastructure that includes surveys of participants, and supports reproducible, content-level, and structurally rich analysis of digital behavior. By combining hierarchical session modeling, content-level capture, and integrated privacy enforcement within a unified system, GESIS Surf provides a general-purpose infrastructure for studying digital behavior in a reproducible manner over time.
institutions: GESIS - Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences

candidates.title: How Does Post-Training Shape LLM Value Preferences?
candidates.abstract: During post-training, large language models (LLMs) learn value preferences from corpora that may contain imbalanced proportions of opinions associated with different demographic groups. Amplifying these imbalances may further underrepresent some groups' opinions. However, how opinion mixtures shape value preferences across post-training paths remains unclear. To answer this question, we conduct controlled experiments using post-training corpora with different opinion mixtures and five post-training paths based on SFT, DPO, and GRPO. We find that post-training amplifies opinion imbalances differently across post-training paths. Once value preferences are amplified, whether further post-training can remove them depends on both the post-training method and the opinion mixture in the corpus. More concerningly, a model's stability under interventions depends on whether further post-training changes its value preference. Moreover, these value preferences are transferred to student models even when distillation uses corpora with no explicit opinion questions. These findings suggest that both the opinion mixture in post-training corpora and the choice of post-training method should be considered when developing, evaluating, and reusing LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ku-nlp/llm-value-preferences.
institutions: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
Singapore University of Technology and Design

candidates.title: Polity size and women’s representation: evidence from two large-scale boundary reforms
candidates.abstract: Abstract Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women’s representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

candidates.title: Gender inclusivity and perceptions of party ideology: Observational and experimental evidence
candidates.abstract: Abstract Do citizens use gender-based heuristics to infer political parties’ ideological positions? We posit that citizens view more ‘gender inclusive’ parties as more left-leaning than comparable male-dominated organizations. Cues about gender inclusivity, moreover, come not only from women’s presence in parties’ legislative delegations but also from other visible signals of women’s incorporation into parties – including as leaders and supporters – and through organizational rules promoting women’s inclusion. We present analyses of election survey data from 21 Western publics over time, which show that, controlling for the left–right tones of parties’ manifestos, citizens perceive more gender-inclusive parties as more left-wing and that the cumulative impact of the various dimensions of gender inclusivity is substantial. We next report experimental evidence from four countries, which provides further support for gender-based heuristics. Our findings highlight the importance of not just the message but also the messenger in shaping citizens’ assessments of parties’ ideological perceptions.

candidates.title: Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
candidates.abstract: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

candidates.title: Incubating Revolution: How Social Networks and the Built Environment Sustain Mobilization
candidates.abstract: How do challengers sustain mobilization under conditions of extreme repression? Social networks and the built environment are critical, interacting at two time scales. Settlement, chain migration, and everyday cooperation produce dense relational environments that shape motivations and constitute latent resources. When contention erupts, those dense social networks can be repurposed to sustain high-risk collective action, providing shelter, escape routes, information, and support. But their efficacy is limited without the organic built environment in which they form; its proximity, limited visibility, and constrained access amplify the effect of dense social ties in facilitating challenge under threat. We substantiate these claims using disaggregated data on protest in Damascus during the 2011 Syrian uprising, finding that neighbourhoods with both dense networks and organic built form exhibit significantly more frequent and confrontational mobilization. By analytically separating the social from the spatial, this article illuminates the mechanisms through which urban neighbourhoods become incubators of rebellion.

candidates.title: Contested terrain: How attitudes toward gender issues relate to voting behavior
candidates.abstract: Abstract While research increasingly links sexist attitudes to far-right support, public debates have moved well beyond women’s equality to encompass LGBTIQ+ rights. Yet studies have been slow to follow, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of attitudes toward trans, intersex, and non-binary people and how they associate with party choice, especially beyond far-right support. Drawing on original data from the German Social Cohesion Panel (2022/23), we are, to our knowledge, among the first to investigate a broader range of gender-related attitudes and find, first, that these constitute two empirically distinct dimensions, binary and non-heteronormative gender issues , that while conceptually intertwined, warrant separate examination. Second, while support for binary gender issues is widespread, non-heteronormative issues remain highly contested. Third, these dimensions relate differently to vote choice: attitudes toward binary gender issues show partisan sorting across the left-right spectrum, while attitudes toward non-heteronormative gender issues reveal a specific antagonism between the Greens and (center-)right parties. Finally, considering both dimensions together uncovers an asymmetry: voters of (center-)right parties form a cohesive conservative bloc, while supportive voters with different attitudinal profiles disperse across (center-)left parties.

candidates.title: Cum-Fake: Improper Dividend Withholding Tax Reclaims Through Pre-Release ADRs
candidates.abstract: Cum-fake schemes use pre-release ADRs without underlying shares to create dividend withholding tax (DWT) refund claims. Using daily ADR data for 2008–2019 and a triple-differences design, we document lending patterns consistent with these schemes. Before 2014, excess dividend-window ADR lending equaled 0.35% of issuer market value in DWT countries, versus 0.04% for U.K. ADRs, where dividends generally face no DWT. This gap vanished after the SEC intensified scrutiny in 2014. ADR and underlying security prices show no persistent wedge. Calibration suggests a tax revenue loss of $264–640 million.

candidates.title: The impact of preference programs in public procurement: Evidence from veteran set-asides
candidates.abstract: Veteran-owned businesses are given preferential treatment in the allocation of procurement contracts from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs – currently the largest civilian federal agency in terms of procurement spending. We exploit a 2016 Supreme Court ruling that significantly increased the scope of these set-asides, to study the impacts of preference programs on both the targeted businesses and procurement outcomes. The policy change increased the share of contracts awarded to the target population, service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses, and benefited not only preexisting vendors but also new entrants, including those who had previously failed to win contracts. We find no evidence of spillovers to awards by other federal agencies, no decline in competition for awards, and no deterioration of contract execution performance by vendors. These findings suggest that VA set-asides have successfully improved outcomes for the target population without imposing significant costs on the government.

candidates.title: Do Political Elites Evaluate Election Outcomes More Favourably than Citizens? Evidence from Parallel Surveys
What Drives Voter Bias Against Muslim Politicians? An Experimental Examination
candidates.abstract: Abstract Religious and ethnic minorities remain underrepresented in political office, but its reasons are debated. Using administrative data from Norwegian local elections, we show that candidates with Muslim names receive fewer personal votes, and propose that this is (partly) due to political beliefs about Muslims as politicians.To examine this claim, we identify salient political beliefs and implement a conjoint experiment that estimates anti-Muslim bias with and without information on these beliefs.In a low-information setting, respondents exhibit a substantial anti-Muslim bias, but providing belief-relevant information reduces this anti-Muslim bias by 2–5 percentage points. The largest reduction occurs when respondents learn candidates’ positions on minority-rights issues. This reduction is driven by right-wing voters and is large enough to eliminate the left-right gap in anti-Muslim bias. These findings show a strong political component in the anti-Muslim bias.
institutions: Norwegian University of Science and Technology

candidates.title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
candidates.abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

candidates.title: Heterogeneous Firms, Growth and the Long Shadows of Business Cycles
candidates.abstract: Do firms differ in their innovation response to business cycles? What economic forces shape this heterogeneity? And does it matter for aggregate propagation? We document substantial heterogeneity in firm-level R&D cyclicality, develop a theory to explain this fact, and validate its key mechanism in the data. In a tractable model of business cycles and innovation-driven growth, endogenous selection makes R&D particularly responsive to aggregate conditions for firms close to the exit margin. Consistent with this mechanism, firms closer to exit display more procyclical R&D in the data. Quantitatively, selection and endogenous growth interact powerfully: selection generates heterogeneous R&D cyclicality, while endogenous growth translates these heterogeneous responses into persistent aggregate effects. Ignoring heterogeneous R&D cyclicality misses roughly half of the long-run output cost of a severe recession.

candidates.title: Do Gender-of-Interviewer Effects Differ Across Immigrant Generations? Survey Evidence from Italy
candidates.abstract: Abstract Interviewer gender has been shown to affect responses to survey questions on gender attitudes and norms, but does its influence vary across groups with different migration backgrounds? I study this question using the Between Origin and Destination (BOnD) survey, conducted in Lombardy, Italy, between 2024 and 2025. Consistent with gender-of-interviewer effects, a type of social desirability bias, female interviewers elicit more progressive responses on a summary index of gender norms and on an index of the acceptability of homosexuality, abortion, divorce, casual sex, and premarital sex. The effect is concentrated among natives and second-generation individuals; first-generation immigrants show little response to interviewer gender. One possible explanation is that social desirability pressure from a female interviewer operates through host-country social norms: Individuals more embedded in the Italian normative context are more responsive to cues from a female interviewer. These findings have implications for the design of surveys administered to mixed native-immigrant populations.

candidates.title: Rebuilding the ship at sea: crisis politics and EU polity formation since 2008
candidates.abstract: The European Union has been in crisis on an ongoing basis since 2008. A wealth of scholarship has charted the contours of the crisis period, often emphasising the EU’s institutional weaknesses and tendency towards sub-optimal or incomplete solutions. Yet the EU has also proven capable of resilience, marshalling both policy and political resources to ‘rebuild the ship at sea’. To understand the cumulative consequences of the post-2008 period for the EU we must understand it as a compound polity, bringing together analyses of both fragility and resilience into a coherent account. The EU polity is characterised by flexible bounding, dispersed binding authority, and second-order bonding, features that can explain its vulnerability to crisis. Yet the same three features can also become sources of adaptability and staying power. This collection presents evidence that Europe’s polity resilience is an established tendency, not just a series of lucky escapes. Crisis politics remains highly contingent, and we cannot assume the EU will always be ‘forged in crisis’ in the sense of progress towards becoming another kind of ideal-type polity. Rather, EU resilience stems from its ability, in a crisis, to hone its apparent weaknesses and turn them into political strengths of collective polity maintenance.
institutions: London School of Economics and Political Science

candidates.title: When Business Speaks, Legislators Listen: Experimental and Qualitative Evidence from Brazil
candidates.abstract: The influence of interest groups on policy making is a central concern in representative democracies, yet identifying causal effects remains a significant challenge. This article argues that legislators respond to informational cues about the economic importance and coalition breadth of interest groups. A field experiment in Brazil, which randomized the receipt of printed and WhatsApp messages from a pro-reform business organization, reveals that legislators are more likely to vote in favor of the group’s position when its membership size, economic importance, and sectoral reach are emphasized. A survey experiment with lobbyists supports this mechanism, showing that messages highlighting group characteristics increase legislators’ expected engagement and support. In-depth interviews with key political figures—including a former president, ministers, and deputies—further corroborate these findings. This study contributes to the literature on informational lobbying and cue-based persuasion by employing realistic experimental treatments and mixed-methods evidence.

candidates.title: Biased Beliefs, Job Search, and Welfare: A Structural Analysis of Coaching and Counseling
candidates.abstract: How do unemployed workers form beliefs about their labor-market prospects, and how do these beliefs affect behavior, policy effectiveness, and welfare? We develop and estimate a structural job-search model with quasi-Bayesian updating, combining Swiss panel data on beliefs and job-search behavior with a randomized counseling-and-coaching intervention. Job seekers enter unemployment with overly optimistic beliefs about interview arrivals, but gradually become pessimistic as past signals fade from memory. The estimated updating process combines features consistent with both motivated beliefs and recency-weighted information processing. The model replicates the observed dynamics of applications, interviews, wages, and job finding, while decomposing treatment effects into changes in search efficiency, search costs, and beliefs. We find that belief formation is the principal channel through which the intervention accelerates transitions into employment. However, despite increasing job finding, the intervention reduces participant welfare because it operates primarily through lower reservation wages.

candidates.title: Increasing healthcare usage among the homeless: Evidence from Mobile Street Clinics in Brazil
candidates.abstract: Homelessness is associated with an immense health burden and limited access to adequate healthcare. This paper studies the effects of Mobile Street Clinics on healthcare usage among people experiencing homelessness in Brazil. Exploiting unique administrative data in a staggered difference-in-differences setting, I find that Mobile Street Clinics strongly and persistently increase primary care usage and psycho-social care usage among people experiencing homelessness but do not improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes. These results suggest that MSCs expand healthcare access and utilization, but that expanding access alone is not sufficient to improve treatment continuity.

candidates.title: Myopia and the Term Structure of Survey Expectations
candidates.abstract: This paper examines evidence for myopia, or cognitive discounting, in macroeconomic models, exploiting information from the term structure of survey expectations. I estimate a Behavioral New Keynesian model, which incorporates, as observable variables, survey forecast data on output, inflation, and interest rates at horizons ranging from one quarter to ten years ahead. When expectations data are excluded, the estimation suggests implausibly large levels of myopia. But when the model is required to match the behavior of expectations in the data, the evidence for myopia largely disappears: the myopia parameter is estimated near one. The extra discounting implied by myopia is, in fact, at odds with the term structure of expectations, which remain quite persistent across horizons, rather than reverting rapidly to steady state. These findings indicate that myopic discounting in New Keynesian frameworks is difficult to reconcile with the dynamics of expectations observed in survey data.

candidates.title: State capacity and wildfire mitigation: Evidence from state-led forest conservation in China
Discussing politics with a chatbot: How political beliefs shape prompt formulation for generative AI
candidates.abstract: By generating comprehensive and highly personalized answers to user prompts, AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini can serve as alternatives to search engines and substantially transform online information seeking. However, little research has examined how users interact with these tools to find information, particularly about politics. In this experiment, we examine how Swiss citizens (N = 563) formulate prompts to search for migration-related issues using AI chatbots and whether this process is affected by selective exposure. We find evidence of attitude-consistent prompting, whereby participants who were more critical of migration were more likely to formulate prompts with an anti-migration stance. This effect was stronger for a broad topic (migration in general) than for a specific one (anti-migration popular initiative put to a vote in Switzerland). However, exposure to an attitude-consistent AI response did not further amplify selectivity in prompting. We also did not find evidence that either AI attitudes or thinking styles moderated selectivity in prompting. These findings contribute to the understanding of selective exposure via AI chatbots and the use of generative AI for political information-seeking.

candidates.title: Jointly Modeling Preferences and Imperfect Decision-Making in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Do preferences Large Language Models (LLMs) express in standard elicitation tasks predict their strategic behaviour? LLM agents interacting with humans and other AI systems face potentially conflicting objectives, such as individual welfare, group welfare, and environmental concerns. Prior work characterizes LLM preferences through behavioral-economic and psychological elicitation or strategic games, but rarely tests consistency across settings and prediction in other strategic environments. This requires modeling how competing objectives jointly shape behavior, whereas existing approaches typically measure preference dimensions in isolation. Drawing on utility theory, we introduce the Preference-Behavior Model (PBM), which combines a preference representation with mechanisms capturing imperfect utility maximization. We formulate estimation as an inverse-game problem, jointly inferring preferences and behavioral parameters from observed choices. We evaluate PBM in three social dilemmas that expose conflicting motives: a Public Goods Game, a Collective-Risk Dilemma, and a Common-Pool Resource dilemma. We find that while preferences estimated from established behavioral economic elicitation instruments do not consistently predict behavior in these dilemmas, models fitted in one dilemma retain predictive value in others, suggesting that inferred preferences capture meaningful aspects of LLM decision-making that elicitation instruments may miss. Finally, we assess alignment with persona instructions, finding that inferred preferences broadly reflect intended priorities with specific divergences across dimensions, LLMs, and games being identified by our approach. Our methodology provides a framework for studying how consistently LLM preferences explain behavior, assessing alignment with intended priorities, and revealing trade-offs and behavioral patterns that standard elicitation may miss.

candidates.title: Should I Mail or Should I Go: Voting Behavior After a One-Time All-Postal Election
candidates.abstract: We investigate how reducing information costs through forced experimentation with postal voting, while holding administrative rules fixed, affects subsequent voting behavior. Leveraging a natural experiment during Bavaria’s 2020 Mayoral Elections and drawing on municipality-level administrative data spanning seven federal and state elections (2013— 2025), we employ an event study design. We find a transitory increase in total turnout of 0.4 percentage points in the first election after the treatment, one and a half years later, and a persistent substitution from in-person to postal voting even five years after the treatment. Municipalities with a higher turnout in the past show larger effects. Investigating the distribution of information costs shows an age gradient, with the highest information costs in the oldest municipalities. The conservative governing party gains from higher postal turnout and other right-wing parties’ in-person voters.

candidates.title: When Firms Lead States: Financial Intermediaries and the Politics of Sovereign Green Bond Issuance
candidates.abstract: Abstract Sovereign green bonds typically appear only after corporate green bond issuance has accumulated—a sequence at odds with the policy consensus that sovereign borrowing anchors debt market development. I argue that the inversion reflects market building by global investment banks. The four banks that authored the Green Bond Principles in 2014 used early private corporate transactions to build the verification practices, pricing conventions, and investor networks needed for a functioning market, then served as lead managers when sovereigns entered, transferring accumulated expertise across the public–private divide. States entered a market whose institutional infrastructure they did not design. The Cox proportional hazards model shows that accumulated corporate issuance significantly accelerates sovereign entry, while government agency issuance delays it by substituting for direct sovereign participation. A bank-level triangulation shows that founding-bank presence at sovereign entry reflects green-bond-specific expertise transfer rather than general dominance in sovereign debt underwriting. The findings identify financial intermediaries as a distinct channel through which sustainable finance reaches sovereign borrowers and show how privately constructed market conditions shape the terms on which states engage with global climate finance.

rising.title: Attacking Women or their Policies? Understanding Violence against Women in Politics
rising.abstract: We present the first causal evidence that female politicians are more likely to face political violence. Using fourteen years of data on attacks against Italian politicians, we show that marginally elected female mayors—similar to men and elected in comparable towns—are three times as likely to be attacked. We find no gender differences in policy platforms, policymaking, performance, or corruption. Instead, violence emerges independently on women's choices, consistently with discrimination - rather than political influence - driving the gap in violence. Female mayors are less likely to seek re-election after attacks, highlighting violence’s role in perpetuating the gender gap.

rising.title: Artificial intelligence in government: why people feel they lose control
rising.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in public administration is expanding rapidly. While AI promises greater efficiency and responsiveness, its integration into government and administration raises concerns about fairness, transparency, and accountability. Relying on principal-agent theory and related frameworks, we conceptualize AI adoption as a case of algorithmic delegation involving power and information asymmetries. This perspective highlights three core tensions: assessability (can the delegate’s decisions be understood?), dependency (can the delegation be reversed?), and contestability (can the delegate’s decisions be challenged?). These structural challenges may lead to a ‘failure-by-success’ dynamic, where early functional gains obscure long-term risks to democratic legitimacy. We conducted a pre-registered factorial survey experiment across tax, welfare, and law enforcement domains. Our findings show that although providing information about efficiency gains initially bolsters trust, it simultaneously reduces citizens’ perceived control. When the structural risks come to the foreground institutional trust and perceived control both drop sharply, suggesting that hidden costs of AI adoption significantly shape public attitudes. The study demonstrates that delegation theory offers a powerful lens for understanding the institutional and political implications of AI in government, emphasizing the need for policymakers to address delegation risks transparently to maintain public trust.

rising.title: The (alleged) consequences of affective polarization: A survey experiment in nine democracies
rising.abstract: Abstract Affective polarization (or antipathy between supporters of opposing political camps) is considered a threat to societal cohesion and democratic stability worldwide. However, causal evidence of its impact remains scarce, especially outside the United States. Our study examines the individual-level consequences of affective polarization by manipulating it in a survey experiment in nine countries (Brazil, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States; N ≈ 18,000) and subsequently assessing the downstream consequences for social avoidance and discrimination of opponents, support for aggression, aversion to political compromise, democratic norms, democratic dissatisfaction, and political engagement. Our intervention successfully reduced participants’ affective polarization in six out of nine countries. In turn, this was associated with significant improvement in interpersonal relations and (in contrast to recent US studies) support for democratic norms. Importantly, the impact varied between societies, suggesting that the consequences of affective polarization may be more context-dependent than previously understood.

rising.title: More social, less material, more influenced by family ties: Why young women join political parties
rising.abstract: Abstract Do young women and men join political parties for different reasons? To investigate, we theorize the following: first, women will be more attracted by social incentives and men by material ones, while purposive incentives will be equally appealing to both; second, before signing up, women will have more party-affiliated family ties than men; and third, these ties will moderate the gender gap in incentives. Drawing on YOUMEM survey data from over 3500 youth wing members of the main center-left and center-right parties in Australia, Austria, Germany, Italy, and Spain, we find strong support for our argument. Our results show that, already in this early – but crucial – part of the pipeline to power, the incentives for joining parties are gendered: young women are more mobilized by social benefits, and less so by material ones. In addition, they are more likely than men to have party-affiliated family ties, indicating that these resources are particularly valuable to them in overcoming the disadvantages they face when entering politics. Notably, family ties boost women’s purposive motivations more than men’s, but they also reduce women’s material motivations to a greater extent. Our findings indicate that if parties are interested in recruiting more young women, they should emphasize the social rewards of membership in their recruitment campaigns.

rising.title: Further Back to the Future: Neo-Royalism, the Trump Administration, and the Emerging International System
rising.abstract: Abstract With the Liberal International Order (LIO) in decline, scholars have focused increasingly on the possible return to a Westphalian great power system marked by sovereigntist claims and balancing among states. The actions of the Trump administration, however, raise a number of significant puzzles for such accounts—the US seems willing to sign deals with traditional adversaries including Russia and China, while targeting long-standing allies like Canada and Denmark. At the same time, transactional politics often serve narrow personalist interests rather than national objectives. In short, a Westphalian lens focused on states and sovereignty may generate intellectual blinders that misreads the emerging international order. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative account, which we label neo-royalism. The neo-royalist order centers on an international system structured by a small group of hyper elites, which we term cliques. Such cliques seek to legitimize their authority through appeals to their exceptionalism in order to generate durable material and status hierarchies based on the extraction of financial and cultural tributes. This short paper lays out the key elements of the neo-royalist order, differentiating it from the Westphalian and Liberal International Orders, and applies its insights to better grapple with the emerging system being promoted by the United States under Donald J. Trump. For policymakers and scholars, the neo-royalist approach clarifies recent events in US foreign policy. Theoretically, the field should take contending ideas of international order seriously, and establish a research agenda beyond a backward looking view to the Westphalian moment.

rising.title: Examining Partisan Asymmetries in Fake News Sharing and the Efficacy of Accuracy Prompt Interventions
rising.abstract: The spread of misinformation has become a central concern in American politics. Recent studies of social media sharing suggest that Republicans are considerably more likely to share fake news than Democrats. However, such inferences are confounded by the far greater supply of right-leaning fake news—Republicans may indeed be more prone to sharing fake news, or they may simply be more exposed to it. This article disentangles these competing explanations by examining sharing intentions in a balanced information environment. Using a large national survey of YouGov respondents, we show that Republicans are indeed more prone to sharing ideologically concordant fake news than Democrats, but that this gap is not large enough to explain differences in sharing observed online. Encouragingly, however, we also find that accuracy prompt interventions that reduce the spread of fake news are equally effective across parties, suggesting that fake news sharing among Republicans is not an intractable problem.

rising.title: Dollar Diminished: The Unmaking of US Financial Hegemony Under Trump
rising.abstract: Abstract The actions of the second Trump administration pose a serious threat to the dominance of the US dollar. Erratic US policies erode global trust in the United States and force states and private actors alike to reconsider their reliance on the dollar. This is reflected across three dimensions of dollar dominance: in trade and payments, as reserve currency and safe asset, and as global investment and funding currency. What distinguishes the current moment from previous predictions of a decline of financial hegemony is that the dollar’s global role is now challenged across all three dimensions simultaneously. Following the Global Financial Crisis, growing uneasiness with US financial power, especially the use of financial sanctions, already created cracks at the margins of the system and prompted a search for alternatives, triggering partial reserve diversification and de-dollarization of trade and payments systems. Under Trump, the undermining of the global economic order, growing fiscal deficits, and continued attacks on the institutional foundations of the administrative state are fundamentally undermining trust in the United States that is fundamental for the dollar’s global role. This signals a rupture in the US-centric global financial system, altering the foundations of the rules-based liberal international order (LIO). However, existing network effects slow down this process and no alternative can yet replace the dollar. The result is a financial interregnum where rising powers seek autonomy and influence without assuming hegemonic responsibility, leading to a more fragmented, multipolar financial order.

rising.title: Correcting measurement error bias in conjoint survey experiments
rising.abstract: Abstract Conjoint survey designs are spreading across the social sciences due to their unusual capacity to estimate many causal effects from a single randomized experiment. Unfortunately, by their ability to mirror complicated real‐world choices, these designs often generate substantial measurement error and thus bias. We replicate both the data collection and analysis from eight prominent conjoint studies, all of which closely reproduce published results, and reveal high levels of measurement error in all. We then discover a common empirical pattern in how measurement error appears in conjoint studies and, with it, introduce an easy‐to‐use statistical method to correct the bias. Along the way, we provide a much simpler and simultaneously more powerful approach to designing, organizing, understanding, and analyzing conjoint data analyses.

rising.title: Interactions in a politicised Europe: a scoping literature review and research agenda on the supranational enforcement of EU law by the European Commission
rising.abstract: Since the 1990s, extensive research has been done on the supranational enforcement of EU law, for good reason; equal application of EU law in member states is crucial to the legitimacy of the Union, the protection of shared interests, and citizens’ rights. Enforcing EU law, primarily a task of the European Commission as ‘guardian of the treaties’, is rife with intra-institutional, inter-institutional, and inter-level interactions. This article presents a scoping literature review of existing studies on the supranational enforcement of EU law, focussing on the actors involved, the interactions between them, and the theoretical approaches used. We identify which interactions remain understudied and shed light on the theoretical emphases in the literature. Finally, we present a research agenda that can inform research into how preferences and understandings concerning enforcement are shaped and changed through interactions of complex actors within and between institutions, thus expanding the theoretical scope of analyses of EU enforcement.

rising.title: Digital Disintegration: Techno-Blocs and Strategic Sovereignty in the AI Era
rising.abstract: Abstract States are reshaping the global digital economy to assert control over the artificial intelligence (AI) value chain. Operating outside multilateral institutions, they pursue measures such as export controls on advanced semiconductors, infrastructure partnerships, and bans on foreign digital platforms. This digital disintegration reflects an elite-centered response to the infrastructural power that private firms wield over critical AI inputs. A handful of companies operate beyond the reach of domestic regulation and multilateral oversight, controlling access to technologies that create vulnerabilities existing institutions struggle to contain. As a result, states have asserted strategic digital sovereignty: the exercise of authority over core digital infrastructure, often through selective alliances with firms and other governments. The outcome is an emergent form of AI governance in techno-blocs: coalitions that coordinate control over key inputs while excluding others. These arrangements challenge the liberal international order by replacing multilateral cooperation with strategic—and often illiberal—alignment within competing blocs.

rising.title: Do geopolitical risks raise or lower inflation?
The global transmission of U.S. monetary policy
Accounting for the profits of multinational enterprises: Double counting and misattribution of foreign affiliate income
rising.abstract: Given the perception that multinational enterprises (MNEs) engage in extensive tax planning, ending base erosion and profit shifting activity is a priority on many national agendas. Yet the actual level of such activity is subject to debate. In this paper, we provide guidance on how to accurately measure country-level MNE income using the datasets commonly used in research on profit shifting. This issue is of global concern, as any economic data that reports profits by jurisdiction must use an established accounting method to report the activity of the MNEs’ indirectly owned foreign affiliates. We explain how the accounting method used could lead a researcher to double count income or to attribute it to the wrong jurisdiction. Such errors not only affect measures of the MNEs’ country-level profits, but also bias researchers’ estimates of the sensitivity of income to taxes. Although we focus our analysis on data from the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), we illustrate the consequences of such mismeasurement across a variety of studies relying on a variety of data sources.

rising.title: The Effect of Omitted Variables on the Sign of Regression Coefficients
rising.abstract: We show that, depending on how the impact of omitted variables is measured, it can be substantially easier for omitted variables to flip coefficient signs than to drive them to zero. This behavior occurs with “Oster's delta” (Oster 2019a), a widely reported robustness measure. Consequently, any time this measure is large—suggesting omitted variables may be unimportant—a much smaller value reverses the sign of the parameter of interest. We propose a modified measure of robustness to address this concern. We illustrate our results in four empirical applications and two meta-analyses. We implement our methods in the companion Stata module “regsensitivity.” (JEL C18, C21, C52)

rising.title: The Macroeconomic Impact of Climate Change: Global Versus Local Temperature
rising.abstract: Abstract This article estimates that the macroeconomic damages from climate change are an order of magnitude larger than previously thought. Exploiting natural global temperature variability, we find that 1ºC warming reduces world GDP by over 20% in the long run. Global temperature correlates strongly with extreme climatic events, unlike country-level temperature used in previous work, explaining our larger estimate. We use this evidence to estimate damage functions in a neoclassical growth model. Business-as-usual warming implies a present welfare loss of more than 30%, and a social cost of carbon in excess of $1,200 per ton. These impacts suggest that unilateral decarbonization policy is cost-effective for large countries such as the United States.
